title: CompTIA A+: Hardware, OS, Troubleshooting
description: For A+ learners reviewing hardware, networking, operating systems, security and troubleshooting fundamentals. Original concept questions, not exam items; verify with current guidelines for electrical safety and device servicing.

cards.front: What is a motherboard?
cards.back: The main circuit board that connects the processor, memory, storage interfaces, expansion devices and power connections.

cards.front: What does the CPU do?
cards.back: Executes program instructions and performs arithmetic, logical and control operations.

cards.front: What is a CPU core?
cards.back: An execution unit within a processor that can process its own instruction stream.

cards.front: What does CPU clock frequency measure?
cards.back: Clock cycles per second; it is one performance factor, not a complete performance rating.

cards.front: What is a hardware thread?
cards.back: An execution context presented by processor hardware to the operating system.

cards.front: What is CPU cache?
cards.back: Small, fast memory near or within the CPU that stores frequently used data and instructions.

cards.front: Why is cache useful?
cards.back: It reduces the average time the CPU waits for memory access.

cards.front: What does RAM provide?
cards.back: Working memory for active programs and data.

cards.front: Is ordinary DRAM volatile?
cards.back: Yes. It loses stored data when power is removed.

cards.front: How does storage differ from RAM?
cards.back: Storage retains files without power; RAM provides faster temporary working space.

cards.front: What is a DIMM?
cards.back: A dual inline memory module, commonly used for desktop memory.

cards.front: What is a SO-DIMM?
cards.back: A smaller memory module commonly used in laptops and compact systems.

cards.front: Can different DDR memory generations normally share the same socket?
cards.back: No. Physical keying and electrical requirements differ.

cards.front: What is dual-channel memory operation?
cards.back: Use of two memory channels to increase potential memory bandwidth with a supported configuration.

cards.front: What is ECC memory?
cards.back: Memory that supports detection and correction of certain data errors when the system supports it.

cards.front: What should be checked before buying replacement RAM?
cards.back: Motherboard compatibility, memory generation, capacity limits, module type and supported configuration.

cards.front: What is a CPU socket?
cards.back: The mechanical and electrical interface that connects a compatible processor to a motherboard.

cards.front: What is thermal interface material used for?
cards.back: It fills microscopic gaps between a chip and heat sink to improve heat transfer.

cards.front: What is a heat sink?
cards.back: A component that conducts and dissipates heat from a device, often with help from airflow.

cards.front: What is thermal throttling?
cards.back: Automatic reduction of performance to keep a component within temperature limits.

cards.front: What can cause a PC to shut down under heavy load?
cards.back: Possible causes include overheating, inadequate power delivery or hardware faults; inspect temperatures and power evidence before replacing parts.

cards.front: What is a PSU?
cards.back: A power supply unit that converts input power into the regulated voltages a computer needs.

cards.front: Why must a replacement PSU have suitable connectors as well as adequate wattage?
cards.back: Components require compatible electrical connections and sufficient power on the needed outputs.

cards.front: Why should modular PSU cables not be assumed interchangeable?
cards.back: The PSU-side pinout can differ even when connectors look identical, risking damage.

cards.front: What does a UPS provide?
cards.back: Temporary battery power during an outage, often with power conditioning and orderly-shutdown support.

cards.front: How does a surge protector differ from a UPS?
cards.back: A surge protector limits transient overvoltage but does not normally supply battery runtime.

cards.front: What is PCI Express?
cards.back: A high-speed serial expansion interconnect organized into lanes.

cards.front: What does a PCIe x16 slot designation describe?
cards.back: A connection with up to sixteen lanes; a physically x16 slot may be wired for fewer lanes.

cards.front: What is an expansion card?
cards.back: A circuit board installed to add functions such as graphics, networking or storage interfaces.

cards.front: What does a GPU specialize in?
cards.back: Highly parallel processing, especially graphics rendering and related workloads.

cards.front: How does integrated graphics differ from a discrete graphics card?
cards.back: Integrated graphics is part of a processor or chipset and often shares system memory; a discrete card is separate hardware.

cards.front: What is firmware?
cards.back: Software stored in nonvolatile memory that controls low-level hardware behavior.

cards.front: What is UEFI?
cards.back: A modern firmware interface that initializes hardware and starts an operating system's boot process.

cards.front: What is POST?
cards.back: Power-on self-test, a firmware-stage hardware check during startup.

cards.front: What might beep codes or diagnostic LEDs indicate?
cards.back: Hardware initialization faults; interpret them using the specific manufacturer's documentation.

cards.front: What does boot order control?
cards.back: The sequence of devices or boot entries firmware tries when starting an operating system.

cards.front: What is Secure Boot?
cards.back: A UEFI feature that checks boot software against trusted signing information to help block unauthorized boot code.

cards.front: What is a TPM?
cards.back: A trusted platform module that protects cryptographic keys and supports security functions such as measured boot.

cards.front: What can a failing RTC battery cause?
cards.back: Loss of clock accuracy or some firmware settings when external power is absent, depending on the system.

cards.front: Why must firmware updates match the exact device model?
cards.back: An incompatible firmware image can render the device unusable.

cards.front: What is an HDD?
cards.back: A hard disk drive that stores data magnetically on rotating platters.

cards.front: What is an SSD?
cards.back: A solid-state drive, usually using flash memory, with no moving read/write mechanism.

cards.front: Why are SSDs generally better at random access than HDDs?
cards.back: They avoid mechanical seek and rotational delays.

cards.front: What is SATA?
cards.back: A storage interface commonly used by hard drives and some solid-state drives.

cards.front: What is NVMe?
cards.back: A storage protocol designed for nonvolatile memory, commonly carried over PCIe.

cards.front: Does an M.2 connector guarantee NVMe support?
cards.back: No. M.2 describes a form factor and connector family; a drive or slot may use SATA, PCIe or other interfaces.

cards.front: What should be checked for an M.2 upgrade?
cards.back: Supported interface, keying, length, firmware support and any lane-sharing restrictions.

cards.front: What is SMART in storage devices?
cards.back: Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology, which exposes drive health information.

cards.front: Does a normal SMART report guarantee a drive will not fail?
cards.back: No. Failures can occur without a prior SMART warning.

cards.front: What is TRIM used for on SSDs?
cards.back: It tells the drive which logical blocks are no longer in use so storage management can be more efficient.

cards.front: What is RAID 0?
cards.back: Striping across drives for capacity and performance, with no redundancy.

cards.front: What is RAID 1?
cards.back: Mirroring data across drives to tolerate an appropriate drive failure.

cards.front: What is RAID 5?
cards.back: Striping with distributed single parity, requiring at least three drives and tolerating one drive failure.

cards.front: What is RAID 6?
cards.back: Striping with distributed double parity, requiring at least four drives and tolerating two drive failures.

cards.front: What is RAID 10?
cards.back: Striping across mirrored sets, usually requiring at least four drives.

cards.front: Why is RAID not a backup?
cards.back: Deletion, corruption, malware or disasters can affect the entire array and its current data.
cards.hint: Consider deletion or ransomware affecting all live copies.

cards.front: What is hot swapping?
cards.back: Replacing a supported component while the system remains powered, following device and controller requirements.

cards.front: What does drive partitioning do?
cards.back: Divides a storage device into logical regions that can hold file systems or other data structures.

cards.front: What is formatting a volume?
cards.back: Creating file-system structures so the operating system can store and organize files.

cards.front: What is GPT?
cards.back: The GUID Partition Table, a modern disk partitioning scheme.

cards.front: What is a file system?
cards.back: The structures and rules used to organize, store and retrieve files on a volume.

cards.front: What is NTFS commonly used for?
cards.back: Windows volumes that need features such as access-control permissions, journaling and large-file support.

cards.front: What is exFAT commonly used for?
cards.back: Removable storage needing large-file support and compatibility across multiple operating systems.

cards.front: What limitation affects an individual file on FAT32?
cards.back: Its maximum file size is just under 4 GiB.

cards.front: What is an optical drive?
cards.back: A drive that uses a laser to read or write supported optical discs.

cards.front: What is USB?
cards.back: A widely used interface for connecting peripherals and supplying power within negotiated limits.

cards.front: Does a USB-C connector guarantee a particular data speed?
cards.back: No. Connector shape alone does not specify supported data, display or power features.

cards.front: What is USB Power Delivery?
cards.back: A specification that allows compatible devices to negotiate power delivery over supported USB connections.

cards.front: What does HDMI commonly carry?
cards.back: Digital video and audio.

cards.front: What does DisplayPort commonly carry?
cards.back: Digital video and audio, with features dependent on the supported version and devices.

cards.front: What does VGA carry?
cards.back: Analog video, normally without audio.

cards.front: What does an Ethernet cable with an 8P8C plug commonly connect?
cards.back: A wired network interface to a switch, router or other Ethernet device.

cards.front: Why are twisted pairs used in copper network cables?
cards.back: Twisting helps reduce electromagnetic interference and crosstalk.

cards.front: What is fiber-optic cable?
cards.back: Cable that carries data as light through glass or plastic fibers.

cards.front: What is an advantage of fiber near electrical interference?
cards.back: The optical data path is immune to electromagnetic interference.

cards.front: What is a docking station?
cards.back: A device that expands a portable computer's connections, possibly including power, displays and networking.

cards.front: What does a laptop digitizer detect?
cards.back: Touch or stylus input over a display surface.

cards.front: What is a backlight's role in a typical LCD?
cards.back: It illuminates the panel so the liquid-crystal image can be seen.

cards.front: What does an OLED display use for light?
cards.back: Its pixels emit light directly rather than relying on a separate LCD backlight.

cards.front: What is a safe response to a swollen lithium-ion battery?
cards.back: Stop using and charging the device, avoid puncturing or compressing it, and arrange qualified handling under current local guidance.

cards.front: What is a network switch's basic role?
cards.back: Forward Ethernet frames within a network using learned MAC-address information.

cards.front: What is a router's basic role?
cards.back: Forward packets between IP networks according to routing information.

cards.front: What is a wireless access point?
cards.back: A device that connects wireless clients to a network.

cards.front: What is a modem's role?
cards.back: It interfaces with a provider's access technology by converting signals as that service requires.

cards.front: What is a firewall?
cards.back: A control that permits or blocks network traffic according to rules and state information.

cards.front: What is a MAC address?
cards.back: A link-layer interface identifier used by technologies such as Ethernet and Wi-Fi.

cards.front: How long is an IPv4 address?
cards.back: 32 bits.

cards.front: How long is an IPv6 address?
cards.back: 128 bits.

cards.front: What does a subnet mask identify in IPv4?
cards.back: Which address bits designate the network portion and which designate the host portion.

cards.front: What does /24 mean in an IPv4 prefix?
cards.back: The first 24 bits are the network prefix, corresponding to 255.255.255.0.

cards.front: What is a default gateway?
cards.back: The next-hop router a host uses for destinations without a more specific route.

cards.front: What is DHCP?
cards.back: A protocol that automatically supplies network configuration such as IP address, gateway and DNS servers.

cards.front: What is DNS?
cards.back: A distributed naming system that resolves names to records such as IP addresses.

cards.front: What is an IPv4 APIPA address often a clue to?
cards.back: A Windows host assigned itself an address in 169.254.0.0/16, often because DHCP was unavailable.

cards.front: What is the IPv4 loopback address commonly used for local testing?
What is the IPv6 loopback address?
What are the three private IPv4 ranges?
What is NAT?
cards.back: Network address translation, which rewrites address information as traffic crosses a network boundary.

cards.front: What is port address translation?
cards.back: A form of NAT that also uses transport-layer port numbers so multiple hosts can share an address.

cards.front: What is a TCP port number used for?
cards.back: To identify an application endpoint within a host's TCP communications.

cards.front: How does TCP differ from UDP?
cards.back: TCP provides connection-oriented, ordered, reliable byte-stream delivery; UDP sends datagrams without built-in delivery guarantees.

cards.front: What service commonly uses TCP port 22?
cards.back: SSH, for encrypted remote access and related services.

cards.front: What service commonly uses TCP port 23?
cards.back: Telnet, a remote terminal protocol without built-in encryption.

cards.front: What service commonly uses TCP port 25?
cards.back: SMTP for mail transfer between servers.

cards.front: What service commonly uses port 53?
cards.back: DNS, using UDP or TCP depending on the operation.

cards.front: What service commonly uses UDP ports 67 and 68?
cards.back: DHCPv4: server port 67 and client port 68.

cards.front: What service commonly uses TCP port 80?
cards.back: HTTP.

cards.front: What service commonly uses TCP port 443?
cards.back: HTTPS over TLS; HTTP/3 commonly uses UDP 443.

cards.front: What service commonly uses TCP port 445?
cards.back: Direct-hosted SMB file and printer sharing.

cards.front: What service commonly uses port 3389?
cards.back: Remote Desktop Protocol; deployments can use TCP and UDP.

cards.front: What service commonly uses TCP port 143?
cards.back: IMAP without implicit TLS; it may be upgraded with STARTTLS if supported and configured.

cards.front: What service commonly uses TCP port 993?
cards.back: IMAP with implicit TLS.

cards.front: What service commonly uses UDP port 123?
cards.back: Network Time Protocol, NTP.

cards.front: What is an SSID?
cards.back: A wireless network name advertised or configured for Wi-Fi access.

cards.front: What is WPA2?
cards.back: A Wi-Fi security generation; secure configurations commonly use AES-based CCMP.

cards.front: What is WPA3-Personal's SAE intended to improve?
cards.back: Password-based authentication, including resistance to offline password-guessing attacks compared with older personal-mode handshakes.

cards.front: Why is hiding an SSID not strong wireless security?
cards.back: The network can still be discovered from wireless traffic; hiding the name does not encrypt or authenticate access.

cards.front: What is a guest wireless network used for?
cards.back: Providing visitor connectivity while separating access from trusted internal resources.

cards.front: What is a VLAN?
cards.back: A logical Layer 2 network segment that separates broadcast domains on supporting equipment.

cards.front: What is a VPN?
cards.back: A virtual private network that creates a protected logical connection across another network.

cards.front: How do bandwidth and latency differ?
cards.back: Bandwidth is transfer capacity; latency is delay before or during communication.

cards.front: What is packet loss?
cards.back: Failure of some transmitted packets to reach their destination.

cards.front: What is network jitter?
cards.back: Variation in packet delay, which can disrupt real-time audio or video.

cards.front: Why can 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi be crowded?
cards.back: Many neighboring networks and non-Wi-Fi devices share the band.

cards.front: Does a stronger Wi-Fi signal guarantee fast internet?
cards.back: No. Congestion, interference, upstream limits or service problems can still reduce throughput.

cards.front: What is a captive portal?
cards.back: A web-based access or acceptance page shown before a network permits normal internet use.

cards.front: What does ping test?
cards.back: Basic IP reachability and round-trip timing through ICMP echo when permitted.

cards.front: Does a failed ping prove a host is offline?
cards.back: No. Firewalls or policies may block ICMP while other services work.

cards.front: What does traceroute or tracert help reveal?
cards.back: The sequence of responding routers along a path and their response times, subject to filtering and routing behavior.

cards.front: What is a likely issue if IP access works but hostnames fail?
cards.back: DNS resolution or name-configuration problems.

cards.front: What is an operating system?
cards.back: System software that manages hardware, processes, memory, storage and user-facing services.

cards.front: What is a kernel?
cards.back: The core part of an operating system that manages critical resources and hardware interaction.

cards.front: What is a device driver?
cards.back: Software that enables the operating system to communicate with a particular hardware device or class.

cards.front: What is a process?
cards.back: A running instance of a program with its own resources and execution state.

cards.front: What is a software thread?
cards.back: A schedulable execution path within a process.

cards.front: What is virtual memory?
cards.back: An abstraction that gives processes address spaces and can use secondary storage to supplement physical RAM.

cards.front: What is paging?
cards.back: Moving fixed-size memory pages between physical memory and backing storage or managing their mappings.

cards.front: Why can excessive paging slow a system?
cards.back: Storage access is much slower than RAM, so frequent page transfers create delays.

cards.front: What is a 64-bit operating system's memory advantage over a typical 32-bit desktop system?
cards.back: It can support much larger address spaces, subject to hardware and edition limits.

cards.front: What does Task Manager help inspect in Windows?
cards.back: Running processes, resource use, startup apps and other system activity.

cards.front: What does Device Manager help inspect in Windows?
cards.back: Installed devices, driver status and reported hardware configuration problems.

cards.front: What does Event Viewer provide?
cards.back: Access to system, application and security event logs.

cards.front: What is Disk Management used for?
cards.back: Viewing and managing disks, partitions, volumes and drive letters.

cards.front: What does Windows Services management control?
cards.back: Background services, their status and startup behavior.

cards.front: What is the Windows Registry?
cards.back: A hierarchical configuration database used by Windows and many applications.

cards.front: Why should Registry edits be carefully scoped and backed up?
cards.back: Incorrect edits can break applications, configuration or boot behavior.

cards.front: What is Safe Mode used for?
cards.back: Troubleshooting with a limited set of drivers and services.

cards.front: What is a clean boot intended to isolate?
cards.back: Conflicts involving startup programs or nonessential services by selectively disabling them.

cards.front: What is System Restore intended to roll back?
cards.back: Supported system configuration, drivers and related system state to a restore point; it is not a personal-file backup.

cards.front: What is Windows Recovery Environment?
cards.back: A recovery environment with tools for startup repair, recovery and troubleshooting outside a normal Windows session.

cards.front: What is the purpose of a recovery key for encrypted storage?
cards.back: It provides an authorized way to unlock data when normal unlock mechanisms cannot be used.

cards.front: Why should recovery keys be secured separately from a device?
cards.back: A lost or failed device should not make the only recovery method unavailable or expose it to the same thief.

cards.front: What does BitLocker provide?
cards.back: Windows volume encryption on supported systems and configurations.

cards.front: What is a local user account?
cards.back: An account defined and authenticated on the individual computer.

cards.front: What is a domain account?
cards.back: An account managed by a directory domain and used to access authorized domain resources.

cards.front: What is the principle of least privilege?
cards.back: Give users and programs only the permissions needed for their tasks.

cards.front: Why use a standard account for routine work?
cards.back: It reduces the scope of accidental changes and some malicious actions compared with unrestricted administrative use.

cards.front: What does User Account Control do?
cards.back: It prompts or controls elevation for actions requiring administrative privileges according to policy.

cards.front: What is an NTFS access-control entry?
cards.back: A permission rule assigning allowed or denied rights to a user or group.

cards.front: What is permission inheritance?
cards.back: Child objects receive applicable permissions from a parent folder or container.

cards.front: When accessing a Windows file over a share, which permissions matter?
cards.back: Both share and file-system permissions; effective access must satisfy both.

cards.front: What is a mapped network drive?
cards.back: A remote share exposed under a drive letter or similar convenient path.

cards.front: What is a UNC path?
cards.back: A Windows network path such as two leading backslashes followed by server name, share name and optional subpath.

cards.front: What does ipconfig display in Windows?
cards.back: IP configuration for network adapters.

cards.front: What does ipconfig /all add?
cards.back: Detailed adapter configuration, including DHCP, DNS and physical-address information.

cards.front: What does ipconfig /renew request?
cards.back: Renewal of DHCP address configuration for applicable adapters.

cards.front: What does ipconfig /flushdns do?
cards.back: Clears the Windows DNS resolver cache.

cards.front: What does nslookup help troubleshoot?
cards.back: DNS name and record resolution by querying DNS servers.

cards.front: What does sfc /scannow do?
cards.back: Checks protected Windows system files and attempts to repair detected corruption.

cards.front: What is DISM used for in Windows servicing?
cards.back: Managing and servicing Windows images, including certain component-store checks and repairs.

cards.front: What does chkdsk examine?
cards.back: File-system and volume consistency; repair behavior depends on selected options.

cards.front: Why back up important data before storage repairs?
cards.back: Repairs modify structures, and a failing device may deteriorate during intensive operations.

cards.front: What does the Windows command dir show?
cards.back: Files and subdirectories in a directory.

cards.front: What does cd do in a command shell?
cards.back: Changes the current directory.

cards.front: What does mkdir do?
cards.back: Creates a directory.

cards.front: What does the Linux command ls show?
cards.back: Directory contents.

cards.front: What does pwd print?
cards.back: The current working directory's path.

cards.front: What does cp do on Unix-like systems?
cards.back: Copies files or directories according to the specified options.

cards.front: What does mv do on Unix-like systems?
cards.back: Moves or renames files or directories.

cards.front: What does rm do on Unix-like systems?
cards.back: Removes directory entries for files, or directories when appropriate options are supplied; it is not a guaranteed secure erase.

cards.front: What does chmod change?
cards.back: Unix-style file permission modes.

cards.front: What does chown change?
cards.back: File or directory ownership on Unix-like systems, subject to privileges.

cards.front: What does sudo allow when policy permits?
cards.back: Execution of a command with another user's privileges, commonly root.

cards.front: What does grep do?
cards.back: Searches input text for lines matching a pattern.

cards.front: What does ps show?
cards.back: Information about processes.

cards.front: What does the Linux command ip help manage?
cards.back: Network interfaces, addresses, routes and related networking state.

cards.front: What is a package manager?
cards.back: Software that installs, updates and removes software packages and tracks dependencies.

cards.front: What is a filesystem mount point?
cards.back: A directory where a filesystem is attached within the operating system's directory tree.

cards.front: What is virtualization?
cards.back: Running isolated computing environments using abstracted hardware resources.

cards.front: What is a hypervisor?
cards.back: Software or firmware that creates and manages virtual machines.

cards.front: What is a type 1 hypervisor?
cards.back: A hypervisor that runs directly on host hardware rather than as an application on a general-purpose host OS.

cards.front: What is a type 2 hypervisor?
cards.back: A hypervisor running on top of a host operating system.

cards.front: What is a virtual machine snapshot?
cards.back: A point-in-time record of VM state used for rollback; it is not a substitute for an independent backup.

cards.front: What is IaaS?
cards.back: Infrastructure as a Service: provisioned computing resources such as virtual machines, storage and networks.

cards.front: What is PaaS?
cards.back: Platform as a Service: a managed application platform on which customers deploy code.

cards.front: What is SaaS?
cards.back: Software as a Service: an application provided as a hosted service.

cards.front: What is cloud elasticity?
cards.back: The ability to expand or shrink resources in response to demand.

cards.front: What is the cloud shared-responsibility model?
cards.back: Provider and customer divide security and management duties according to the service model and contract.

cards.front: What is mobile device management?
cards.back: Centralized policy, configuration and lifecycle management of enrolled mobile devices.

cards.front: What is a remote wipe?
cards.back: An authorized command intended to erase managed data or device data if the device can receive and execute it.

cards.front: What is MFA?
cards.back: Authentication using two or more distinct factor types, such as knowledge and possession.

cards.front: Why are two passwords not two-factor authentication?
cards.back: Both are the same factor type: something you know.

cards.front: What is phishing?
cards.back: A deceptive message or interaction intended to make a person reveal information or perform an unsafe action.

cards.front: What is spear phishing?
cards.back: Phishing tailored to a particular person or organization.

cards.front: What is social engineering?
cards.back: Manipulating people to obtain access, information or actions that bypass normal controls.

cards.front: What is tailgating in physical security?
cards.back: Following an authorized person into a restricted area without proper authorization.

cards.front: What is ransomware?
cards.back: Malware that extorts victims, often by encrypting data or threatening data disclosure.

cards.front: What is a trojan?
cards.back: Malicious software presented as legitimate or desirable software.

cards.front: How does a worm differ from a typical virus?
cards.back: A worm can propagate independently across systems; a virus attaches to host content and spreads through its execution or use.

cards.front: What is a rootkit?
cards.back: Software designed to hide malicious activity or maintain privileged access through stealthy system changes.

cards.front: What is encryption?
cards.back: Transforming data using an algorithm and key so it is unreadable without authorized decryption.

cards.front: What is hashing?
cards.back: Producing a fixed-size digest from input data, commonly for integrity checking or password-verification schemes.

cards.front: How does hashing differ from encryption?
cards.back: Hashing is not intended to be reversed; encryption is designed to be reversed with the appropriate key.

cards.front: What does a digital signature help verify?
cards.back: Data integrity and the origin associated with the signing key.

cards.front: What is an antivirus quarantine?
cards.back: Isolation of suspicious files so they cannot normally execute while investigation or remediation occurs.

cards.front: What is patch management?
cards.back: A controlled process for assessing, deploying and verifying software updates.

cards.front: Why should unsupported software be replaced or otherwise addressed?
cards.back: It may no longer receive fixes for newly discovered security flaws.

cards.front: What is a strong backup restoration test?
cards.back: Recover selected data in a safe environment and verify it is complete, readable and usable.

cards.front: What is a full backup?
cards.back: A backup of all selected data.

cards.front: What is an incremental backup?
cards.back: A backup of changes since the most recent applicable backup, usually full or incremental.

cards.front: What is a differential backup?
cards.back: A backup of changes since the most recent full backup.

cards.front: What is RPO?
cards.back: Recovery point objective: the maximum tolerable data-loss interval measured backward from a disruption.

cards.front: What is RTO?
cards.back: Recovery time objective: the target time to restore a service after disruption.

cards.front: What is an offline backup's security benefit?
cards.back: It is disconnected from normal systems, reducing exposure to attacks that reach online backups.

cards.front: What is the first goal when identifying a reported computer problem?
cards.back: Gather symptoms, scope, timing, recent changes and user impact before selecting a fix.

cards.front: Why should a technician test a likely cause?
cards.back: To confirm or reject the explanation using evidence before making unnecessary changes.

cards.front: What should be considered before implementing a repair?
cards.back: Its likely effects, data protection needs, authorization, rollback options and user disruption.

cards.front: What comes after applying a fix?
cards.back: Verify full functionality, check related effects and document the outcome.

cards.front: What should a support ticket record?
cards.back: Symptoms, environment, diagnostic evidence, actions, results and any follow-up needed.

cards.front: Why change one variable at a time when practical?
cards.back: It makes cause and effect easier to identify and rollback easier to manage.

cards.front: What is a known-good component used for?
cards.back: Controlled substitution to help determine whether the original component is faulty.

cards.front: What should you check first when a desktop shows no power?
cards.back: External power, outlet, power cable, switches and visible indicators, without opening hazardous power components.

cards.front: What should you check when a powered-on PC has no display?
cards.back: Monitor power and input, cable connections, correct video port and available diagnostic indicators.

cards.front: What should you do before reseating internal PC components?
cards.back: Shut down, disconnect power and follow manufacturer procedures and electrostatic-discharge precautions.

cards.front: What is ESD?
cards.back: Electrostatic discharge, which can damage sensitive electronic components.

cards.front: What is an ESD wrist strap intended to do?
cards.back: Equalize electrical potential with an appropriate grounded work surface when used correctly on de-energized equipment.

cards.front: Why should a technician not open a PC power supply for routine repair?
cards.back: Internal capacitors and circuitry can retain dangerous energy; replace or refer it for qualified service.

cards.front: What is a sensible first response to a clicking HDD with important data?
cards.back: Minimize further use and prioritize data recovery or backup under an appropriate plan.

cards.front: What can cause repeated memory-related crashes?
cards.back: Faulty RAM, incompatible settings, overheating, drivers or other hardware faults; test systematically rather than assuming one cause.

cards.front: What should be checked when a printer is shown as offline?
cards.back: Power, physical or network connection, selected printer, queue state and device status.

cards.front: What does a printer spooler do?
cards.back: Queues and manages print jobs before or while they are sent to a printer.

cards.front: What is duplex printing?
cards.back: Printing on both sides of a sheet.

cards.front: What consumable supplies the image material in a laser printer?
cards.back: Toner.

cards.front: What does a laser printer's fuser do?
cards.back: Uses heat and pressure to bond toner to the paper.

cards.front: What does an inkjet printer deposit on paper?
cards.back: Small droplets of liquid ink.

cards.front: What is a direct thermal printer's main paper requirement?
cards.back: Heat-sensitive paper that darkens where the print head heats it.

cards.front: What often causes repeating marks at regular intervals on laser output?
cards.back: A defect or contamination on a rotating imaging component; spacing can help identify the component.

cards.front: What should be checked for faded laser print?
cards.back: Toner level, print settings and relevant imaging components, following the model's service guidance.

cards.front: What should be checked when a laptop will not charge?
cards.back: Power source, compatible charger rating, cable, port condition and battery or charging status.

cards.front: Why verify the user's data after resolving a profile or login issue?
cards.back: A successful login alone does not prove expected files, settings and permissions are intact.

cards.front: What is the appropriate response when an issue exceeds your authority or expertise?
cards.back: Document findings and escalate through the approved support process.

cards.front: Why is a change log useful during troubleshooting?
cards.back: It links modifications to observed results and supports recovery and later review.
